summary: We developed a web application focused on monitoring the spread, detection, and potential causes of wildfires using data collected by satellite sensors (MODIS and VIIRS). By gathering historical data and comparing it with real-time observations, the platform provides a better understanding of how wildfires and other natural disasters develop and evolve over time. This enables more timely analysis and informed decision-making, helping prevent and mitigate large-scale wildfires while protecting biodiversity, human lives, and our planet.
details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

Satflame combines fire hotspots detected by NASA's MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) satellites into a single comparable time series, presenting the data through a year × month activity calendar and a full-screen interactive map. It addresses the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge, "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots."

The problem: VIIRS provides greater detail (375 m compared to 1 km) and detects approximately four times as many hotspots as MODIS for the same fire. Without adjustment, raw data for the Dominican Republic jumps from 2,155 hotspots in 2011 to 8,331 in 2012 simply because of the change in satellite sensor.

How it works, step by step:

  1. Downloads annual country-level files from NASA FIRMS (MODIS 2000–2025, VIIRS 2012–2025) and completes the current year using the FIRMS area API.
  2. Filters fixed heat sources (factories, volcanoes, oil platforms) and low-confidence detections.
  3. Groups each detection into approximately 1 km grid cells and counts each cell only once per day ("cell-days"), preventing the same fire from being counted multiple times by VIIRS.
  4. Calibrates a factor k using the years in which both sensors overlap (2012–2025), bringing MODIS data to the VIIRS scale: k = 4.69 for the Dominican Republic, with a confidence interval of 4.52–4.89 and R² = 0.905.
  5. Calculates the historical median for each month and its anomaly: how many times more (or less) fire activity is occurring compared to normal levels.
  6. Displays everything through two maps: Global (any country worldwide, loaded on demand) and Local (the Dominican Republic, including provinces and municipalities).

On the map, users can select layers just as they would in FIRMS (basemaps, daily satellite imagery, snow, aerosols, and hotspots by satellite). They can also access eight tools (measurement, location, layers, timeline, capture, sharing, help, and 2D/globe view) and open the History panel, which includes the harmonized calendar and CSV downloads.

When selecting a hotspot, users can view the actual satellite image from that day (NASA GIBS), weather conditions (NASA POWER), the probable direction of fire spread, and an explanation of its likely cause.

An AI assistant answers questions using only the application's data and NASA webpages.

What Are Its Benefits?

It makes it possible to fairly compare wildfire activity from 2000 to the present without being misled by changes in satellite sensors, while making the information understandable even to non-experts.

Who Benefits

Benefits

Emergency managers and Civil Defense

Identify critical fire seasons within seconds and determine whether the current month is above normal (e.g., October 2026 = 0.83 times the median in the Dominican Republic).

Firefighters and response teams

Access the exact hotspot location, detection time, satellite imagery from that day, and wind direction to estimate where the fire may spread.

Scientists and meteorologists

Download the harmonized historical time series in CSV format, including the calibration factor, its uncertainty, and the R² value.

Farmers and landowners

Identify areas that burn each season and determine whether their land follows a recurring fire pattern.

General public

Access a clear map showing what is happening in their province or municipality, in Spanish and without technical jargon.

Students and educators

Understand how satellites detect fires and why data adjustment is necessary.

Additionally, the application works with previously downloaded data even without an Internet connection, and anyone can share the exact map view they are viewing through a link.

What Is the Project's Impact?

Satflame eliminates the artificial jump in the wildfire data series: in the Dominican Republic, raw hotspot counts increase from 2,155 (2011) to 8,331 (2012) due to the change in satellite sensors, while the harmonized series goes from 8,002 to 5,720, without an artificial jump. This makes year-to-year comparisons more reliable and prevents misleading conclusions.

  • Better-informed decisions: Those responsible for prevention planning can identify whether a particular year or month is truly anomalous and allocate response teams and prevention campaigns during critical seasons.
  • Validated data: 149,080 hotspots from the Dominican Republic imported (2000–2025), plus 2026 data. The calibration explains 90.5% of the monthly variation between sensors (R² = 0.905).
  • Global reach: The same methodology works for any of the 177 countries available on the map, with data loaded on demand from FIRMS.
  • Historical data continuity: MODIS is approaching the end of its operational lifespan. Harmonization with VIIRS preserves more than 25 years of comparable historical records.
  • Future vision: A public alert system that notifies people near active fires, as well as firefighters and police, providing location, detection time, and possible fire spread information (currently proposed as an idea, without a working prototype).
What Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware, and Software Were Used?

A web application built with TypeScript and Next.js, using a local SQLite database, developed on a Windows 11 Pro PC and supported by two AI programming assistants.

Category

Technologies and Tools Used

Programming Languages

TypeScript (application and server), SQL (queries), CSS (styling), JSON/GeoJSON (geographic data)

Framework and Interface

Next.js 16 and React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, custom components and design tokens

Maps and Charts

MapLibre GL 6 (2D map and globe), three.js (3D globe on the landing page), Recharts (charts), Turf.js (geographic calculations)

Data and Server

SQLite with better-sqlite3 and Drizzle ORM, Papa Parse (CSV processing), Zod (validation)

Artificial Intelligence

Claude (Anthropic) with its official SDK for the application's assistant; Claude Code and Codex as the team's programming assistants

NASA Data Sources

FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS hotspots), GIBS (satellite imagery and layers), POWER (daily weather data), Visible Earth (globe texture)

Additional Sources

Esri (basemaps), UNEP-WCMC (protected areas), Smithsonian GVP (volcanoes), Natural Earth and geoBoundaries (geographic boundaries)

Testing and Quality

Vitest (111 automated tests), Playwright (end-to-end testing), strict TypeScript

Hardware

Windows 11 Pro PC and Node.js 22; no cloud servers required

Version Control

Git

How Is the Project Innovative?

Satflame takes the concept of NASA FIRMS further: beyond displaying hotspots, it explains what they mean, compares them with historical records, and provides context in a way that anyone can understand.

  • "Raw ↔ Harmonized" toggle: Users can directly see the artificial jump in 2012 and how it disappears after harmonization.
  • Fire activity calendar with anomalies: Each month is color-coded according to how many times fire activity exceeds normal levels, with its numerical value displayed on hover and an equivalent table available for screen readers.
  • Features FIRMS does not provide: Actual satellite imagery from the day of each hotspot, daily weather conditions, probable fire spread direction, and an explained probable cause in simple language (for example, "The area burned in three different years during the same season: a pattern commonly associated with agricultural burning"). These are always presented as probabilities, never as confirmed facts.
  • AI assistant with sources: Answers questions by consulting the database and NASA webpages only, without inventing statistics.
  • Map-centered design: A full-screen interface similar to FIRMS, but with fewer visible options at a time (Hick's Law), an icon toolbar that expands on hover, and a landing page featuring a 3D globe displaying hotspots from the past week.
  • Two perspectives in one application: Global for research and Local for the Dominican public.
What Factors Did the Team Consider?

The team prioritized making the results scientifically defensible, understandable to everyone, and transparent about what is not known.

  • Scientific validity: Fixed heat sources and low-confidence detections are excluded. The calibration publishes its uncertainty (95% CI) and goodness of fit (R²). The years 2000–2002, which have data from only one satellite, receive a separate adjustment factor and a visible warning.
  • Fair comparisons: The "This month vs. median" indicator uses the most recent completed month because an ongoing month would appear artificially low.
  • Honesty about causes: Satellites detect heat, not its cause. The application identifies probable causes and explains the reasoning behind them.
  • Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA): Verified contrast, keyboard navigation, shortcuts, plain-language text, a list alternative to the map, and support for users who prefer reduced motion.
  • Hick's Law: Only a few actions are visible at a time, layer groups are collapsible, and default values are already selected.
  • Data sources and licensing: NASA provides the satellite data. Third-party basemaps and reference layers (Esri, UNEP-WCMC, Smithsonian) are used with attribution and documented on the credits page.
  • Offline functionality: Data is stored locally. If a basemap fails to load, the application automatically switches to a local background and notifies the user.
  • Privacy and security: No analytics or telemetry; FIRMS and AI API keys never reach the browser; the image proxy only accepts authorized layers.
  • Acknowledged limitations: Cloud cover, satellite overpass times, and small fires may prevent some detections. The Suomi NPP satellite stopped publishing data on November 2, 2026, and the application clearly indicates this limitation.
